about.note: The Town of Ossipee, Carroll County (2020 census 4,338), covers the villages of Center Ossipee, Ossipee (Ossipee Corner), West Ossipee and Water Village. Since the March 10, 2026 town election it has been run by a five-member Board of Selectmen (expanded from three by a petitioned article voters passed in March 2025) with a Town Administrator, and voters decide the budget at a traditional Town Meeting the day after the town election. Fire protection comes from three separate fire precincts (Center Ossipee, Ossipee Corner and West Ossipee). The town website (ossipee.org) refused automated access to most of its pages, including Selectmen minutes, the 2026 warrant, the Town Meeting results and the tax rate page, so no 2026 Selectmen minutes were read. Meetings and issues here come from Conway Daily Sun reporting (some reposted by the Ossipee Lake Alliance), AI-written Citizen Portal summaries of meeting videos, and the town PDFs that could be opened (an April 2026 Planning Board agenda and Economic Development Council minutes). The 2026 operating budget amount was not found. Plain-English summaries written by AI; items with needs_review=true are uncertain.

issues.title: Deer Cove Road: voters ended town maintenance of the dead-end section
issues.status: Approved 65-58 at a special town meeting in October 2026; the section becomes a Class VI road
issues.summary: Deer Cove Road runs from Route 16 (across from Aubuchon Hardware) along Ossipee Lake's Deer Cove. The town said the section from South Shore Road north to its dead end has become hard and unsafe to plow because there is no safe turnaround for highway trucks, and owners have built walls, decks and platforms in the right of way. Voters agreed to make that section Class VI: it stays a public road, but the town no longer has to maintain it.
points: December 2025: the Selectmen voted to put the discontinuation on the March 2026 warrant (AI summary of the meeting video).
March 2026 Town Meeting: voters tabled a similar article so officials and owners could look for a solution.
July 3: about 80 people attended a public meeting; owners offered to remove structures in the way of road work.
Public Works Director TJ Eldridge estimated needed improvements (paving, drainage and other work) at $250,000 to $300,000.

The dispute that was not resolved: a year-round public turnaround at the dead end. A 1916 layout set a 16.5-foot right of way with a turnaround; one owner offered a winter-only turnaround on a driveway.

September 21: the Selectmen voted unanimously to send the question to a special town meeting. Selectmen Emery and Rines said that did not mean they favored the change; Rines said at the meeting he personally opposed it.
Special town meeting: 65 yes, 58 no (123 ballots).

issues.title: A rail trail on the Conway Branch line through Ossipee
issues.status: State considering a 2.8-mile gravel trail next to the rails between Ossipee village and Route 16; Selectmen support removing the rails
issues.summary: The Conway Branch rail line runs about 20 miles from Ossipee toward Conway, and the state now manages it through the Department of Natural and Cultural Resources (DNCR). Ossipee's Selectmen voted to support removing the rails on a downtown stretch to build an accessible trail. The state Bureau of Trails instead proposed a quicker first step: a gravel trail beside the rails, which could open by fall 2026.
points: April 2026: on Selectman Copeland's motion, the board voted 5-0 to support removing the rails between Moultonville Road and Route 16 (meeting date not given in the report).
May 6: about 40 people attended the Conway Branch Rail Trail Advisory Committee meeting at the Freight House.
Proposal: a 2.8-mile, 8-foot-wide gravel trail on the east side of the rail, built with state crews and state money. No cost figures were given.
The Bureau of Trails said removing the rails would require public bidding and would not happen in 2026; DNCR's acting commissioner decides whether to go ahead.
The Cotton Valley Rail Trail Club urged keeping as much rail as possible.
Chair Jonathan Smith, also a state representative, sponsored HB 1468, which directs a Conway Branch Rail Line Master Plan.
The town's news list includes 'Three Mile Rail Trail right around the corner' (updated May 9, 2026) and a 'Leaves & Legends' event on October 17, 2026.

issues.title: Police department: a new chief, and the ICE 287(g) agreement
issues.status: James Sullivan named police chief in June 2026; the status of the department's 287(g) agreement with ICE after the change was not found
issues.summary: The Ossipee Police Department had a 287(g) agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (a federal program that lets local officers help with immigration enforcement). At the March 2026 Town Meeting voters passed a non-binding petitioned article asking the department to end it. In April the Selectmen ended Chief Donald Babbin's employment, and in June they named Detective James Sullivan chief.
points: Article 26 (petitioned) recommended ending the 287(g) contract; it passed 75-56. A statewide fact check describes the 2026 town votes on these agreements as non-binding.
Chief Babbin said the program had been used once to make an arrest, and that he had no plans to withdraw.
April 20: the Selectmen voted, after a nonpublic session, to end the chief's employment (vote count not reported).
May: Chair Smith announced Detective James Sullivan as interim chief and Cpl. Will French as interim lieutenant.
June 5: the Selectmen named Sullivan chief (Daily Sun photo caption). The town posted 'Ossipee celebrates new Police Chief and Lieutenant' on June 26.
January 2026: the Selectmen accepted a $13,300 state Highway Safety grant (AI summary of meeting video).

issues.title: Sewer lagoons must close, and water and sewer rates
issues.status: Town planning for the state-required closure of its sewage lagoons (about 2030); rate increases discussed
issues.summary: Ossipee runs town water and sewer systems paid by user fees. The NH Department of Environmental Services (NHDES) is expected to require closing or overhauling the town's sewage lagoons, around 2030. Officials have proposed raising water and sewer rates to build reserves and hiring a consultant to plan the closure.
points: October 2025: officials proposed about a 10% increase to both base rates and usage charges for water and sewer accounts; no vote was taken then.
January 13, 2026: the Public Works Director said NHDES renewed the lagoon permit for five years and will grant no further extensions.

He recommended a consultant-led closure plan and sewer rate study, through a warrant article of up to $100,000 that could be fully reimbursed if program money is secured. Board members asked whether it could be paid from general taxes or must come from sewer users; staff were sent to get legal advice and firmer costs.
Rising costs cited: valves, caps, chemicals, pump station electrical parts and a Door Street main break.

issues.title: Mill Pond swimming hole closed because of a hole in the dam
issues.status: Closed by the Selectmen on May 4, 2026; caution tape put up
issues.summary: The Selectmen closed a popular swimming spot by the Mill Pond dam in Center Ossipee after Public Works warned that a large opening in the dam could pull a swimmer through. The rest of Mill Pond (dock, picnic area and fishing access) was not part of the closure.
points: The closed area is across Moultonville Road from the main pond, near Paddy Acre Road.
Chair Smith cited state dam requirements and said the whole area should be assessed, rebuilt and fenced.
Selectman Ryder said safety must come first until a solution is found; Selectman Copeland said losing the spot would be a big deal.
No repair plan or cost was reported.

issues.title: A new five-member Board of Selectmen and how it runs its meetings
issues.status: Five-member board seated after the March 10, 2026 election
issues.summary: Ossipee went from three selectmen to five this year, under a petitioned article voters passed in March 2025. Thirteen people ran for the three open seats. The board has since changed its meeting rules and times, and Town Meeting turned down a proposal to bar selectmen from working for the town.
points: Board after the election: Jonathan Smith (chair), Kyle Copeland (vice chair), Jim Rines, Wendy Ryder and Dallas Emery.
January 13 (old three-member board): any majority of members may call a meeting and any member may add agenda items; speakers must give name and address, and residents speak before non-residents.
March 16: the new board voted unanimously to move meetings to 5:30 PM to draw more residents. The town calendar later listed the September 21 meeting at 3:30 PM.

Town Meeting: Article 29 (petitioned), which would have barred selectmen from town jobs or contracts other than the selectman's salary, was amended and then defeated 80 yes to 78 no by secret ballot. Chair Smith is also the town's building inspector and zoning enforcement officer.

The state is expected to require closing or overhauling the town's sewage lagoons around 2030; water and sewer are paid by user fees, and a roughly 10% rate increase was proposed in October 2025.
In late 2025 the Selectmen authorized a $3,240,000 tax anticipation note (a short-term loan until taxes come in) with Bank of New Hampshire at 4.875% (AI summary).
